Numerically 10/√3 ≈ 5.77 units, so option A is correct.
Option D (5) would imply cosθ = 0.5 (θ = 60°) and therefore does not satisfy the three‑axis condition cosθ = 1/√3.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A body starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 ms⁻² for 5 seconds. The distance covered is
records.explanation:
Uniformly accelerated motion with initial speed u is described by s = ut + ½at², where s is displacement, a is acceleration and t is time.
Here u = 0, a = 2 m s⁻² and t = 5 s, so s = 0·5 + ½·2·5² = ½·2·25 = 25 m.
Option A is correct because it matches this direct calculation and yields 25 m.
Option D (20 m) is simply an arithmetic miscalculation of ½·2·5²; the correct product ½·2·25 equals 25, not 20.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A stone is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of 20 ms⁻¹. The maximum height reached is (g = 10 ms⁻²)
records.explanation:
The problem involves vertical motion under constant acceleration where maximum height occurs when the upward velocity becomes zero.
Use v^2 = u^2 − 2gh with u = 20 m/s and v = 0, giving 0 = 400 − 20h and hence h = 20 m.
Therefore option A (20 m) is correct because it follows directly from the kinematic equation for displacement under gravity.
Option D (10 m) comes from using h = u/g or confusing distance with the time to reach maximum height (u/g = 2 s), so it is not applicable.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A projectile is fired at 45° to the horizontal with speed u. Its range on a horizontal plane is
records.explanation:
For standard projectile motion on a horizontal plane with no air resistance and equal launch and landing elevation, the range is R = u^2 sin2θ / g.
At θ = 45°, sin2θ = sin90° = 1, so R = u^2/g, which matches option A.
Option B, u^2/2g, is the formula for maximum height (more generally u^2 sin^2θ /(2g)), not horizontal range.
These conclusions rely on constant g and negligible air drag; if launch and landing heights differ or drag matters the simple formula must be modified.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A ball is kicked horizontally from a cliff 45 m high with a velocity of 15 ms⁻¹. How far from the base of the cliff does it land? (g = 10 ms⁻²)
records.explanation:
This is a horizontal projectile problem where vertical motion is free fall under g and horizontal motion is at constant speed, so the two components are independent.
Use the vertical equation h = ½gt²: 45 = ½(10)t² gives t² = 9 and hence t = 3 s.
Horizontal range = horizontal speed × time = 15 m s⁻¹ × 3 s = 45 m, so option A is correct.
Option D (60 m) corresponds to t = 4 s (15×4) and would require a height of ½·10·4² = 80 m, so it is also incorrect.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Newton's first law of motion is a statement about
records.optionsJson: ["The relationship between force and acceleration","The conservation of momentum","Inertia and the tendency of bodies to resist change in motion","Action and reaction forces ✓"]
records.explanation:
Newton's first law states that a body at rest or moving with constant velocity will remain so unless acted upon by a net external force.
This property is called inertia, the tendency of a mass to resist changes in its state of motion.
Option C is correct because it names inertia and the resistance to change in motion, which is the essence of the first law.
Option D is incorrect because action and reaction pairs are the subject of Newton's third law, which describes equal and opposite forces between interacting bodies.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A body of mass 5 kg moving at 6 ms⁻¹ collides with a stationary body of mass 3 kg. If they move together after collision, their common velocity is
records.explanation:
Conservation of linear momentum applies because no external horizontal force is specified, so total momentum before collision equals total momentum after.
Initial momentum is 5 kg×6 m/s = 30 kg·m/s; after the perfectly inelastic collision the combined mass is 5+3 = 8 kg, giving v = 30/8 = 3.75 m/s.
Option A (3.75 m/s) is correct because it follows directly from 30 = 8v and standard momentum conservation for bodies that stick together.
Option D (6 m/s) incorrectly treats the stationary 3 kg body as if it had no effect, which violates conservation of momentum for the closed two-body system.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg mass for 3 seconds starting from rest. The impulse of the force is
records.explanation:
Impulse J is defined as the product of force and time, J = F·t, and equals the change in momentum Δp.
Here J = 20 N × 3 s = 60 N·s.
Alternatively, acceleration a = F/m = 20/4 = 5 m/s² so final speed v = a·t = 5×3 = 15 m/s and Δp = m·v = 4×15 = 60 N·s.
Option C (240 Ns) incorrectly multiplies by mass (F·m·t), and D (80 Ns) is F·m (=20×4) which ignores time; neither represents impulse.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Simple harmonic motion is defined as motion in which the acceleration is
records.optionsJson: ["Constant and directed towards a fixed point","Proportional to displacement and directed towards the equilibrium position","Proportional to velocity and in the same direction as motion","Inversely proportional to displacement ✓"]
records.explanation:
Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is motion where acceleration is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and always directed towards the equilibrium position (a = −ω²x or a = −(k/m)x).
The negative sign indicates the acceleration is a restoring acceleration opposite to displacement, which produces oscillatory motion about the equilibrium point.
Option B is correct because it matches the defining relation for SHM and leads to sinusoidal time-dependence of displacement and velocity.
Option D is incorrect because acceleration inversely proportional to displacement would diverge near the equilibrium and cannot yield the simple sinusoidal oscillations characteristic of SHM.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: In SHM, a particle has maximum velocity when
records.optionsJson: ["Displacement is maximum","Acceleration is maximum © The Scholars Forge Tutorial | 350+ is ours! | Page 8 UTME '26 REVELATION | PHYSICS MASTERY PACK | 200 Questions | Tutor Dave","Displacement is zero (at equilibrium)","Frequency is maximum ✓"]
records.explanation:
In simple harmonic motion (SHM) the particle's speed is v = ω√(A² − x²), where A is amplitude and x is displacement from equilibrium.
This formula shows v is largest when x = 0, because √(A² − 0) = A, so speed is maximum at the equilibrium position.
Acceleration in SHM is a = −ω²x, hence acceleration is zero at equilibrium and has maximum magnitude at x = ±A.
Therefore the correct answer is ‘Displacement is zero (at equilibrium)’ since kinetic energy and speed reach their maximum there.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The area under a velocity-time graph represents
records.optionsJson: ["Acceleration","Force","Displacement","Power ✓"]
records.explanation:
A velocity–time graph shows how an object's velocity varies with time, and the area under the curve equals the time integral of velocity.
Mathematically the area under a v–t curve is ∫v dt, which gives displacement (change in position) with SI units of metres (m).
Acceleration is not the area but the gradient (slope) of a v–t graph because a = dv/dt.
Therefore the correct option is Displacement since integrating velocity over time yields net change in position, while the other choices correspond to slope or different derived quantities.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A car travels the first half of a journey at 60 kmh⁻¹ and the second half at 40 kmh⁻¹. The average speed for the entire journey is
records.explanation:
This problem concerns average speed for equal distances travelled at two different velocities, which uses the harmonic mean rather than the arithmetic mean.
For two equal distances d, total distance = 2d and total time = d/60 + d/40, so average speed = (2d)/(d/60 + d/40) = 2/(1/60 + 1/40).
Compute 2/(1/60 + 1/40) = 2/( (2+3)/120 ) = 2/(5/120) = 48 kmh⁻¹, so option A is correct.
Option D (100 kmh⁻¹) is merely the sum of the two speeds and not a valid average; average speed must be total distance divided by total time.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Resonance occurs in forced vibration when
records.optionsJson: ["The applied frequency equals the natural frequency of the system","The amplitude of vibration is zero","The driving force is removed","Damping is at maximum"]
records.explanation:
In forced vibration an external periodic force drives a system and resonance is the condition where the system responds with the largest steady-state amplitude.
Resonance occurs when the driving (applied) frequency matches the system's natural frequency, giving efficient energy transfer and maximal amplitude, so option A is correct.
Option B is wrong because zero amplitude means no vibration at all, whereas resonance is characterised by large, not zero, amplitude.
Thus the defining feature of resonance in forced vibrations is equality of applied and natural frequencies, with damping determining the peak amplitude but not the resonance condition itself.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A body of mass 2 kg is moving at 10 ms⁻¹. A force brings it to rest in 2 seconds. The magnitude of the retarding force is
records.explanation:
Use Newton's second law and kinematics to find acceleration from the change in velocity over time.
The deceleration is a = (0 − 10)/2 = −5 m·s⁻², so its magnitude is 5 m·s⁻².
Applying F = ma gives F = 2 kg × 5 m·s⁻² = 10 N, directed opposite the motion so the magnitude is 10 N.
Option C (5 N) omits multiplying by the mass, and option D (40 N) has no basis in the kinematic or dynamic calculations.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: At the surface of the Earth, the gravitational field intensity is approximately 10 Nkg⁻¹. At a height equal to the Earth's radius above the surface, the gravitational field intensity is
records.explanation:
Gravitational field intensity g at distance r from the Earth's centre follows the inverse-square law g ∝ 1/r².
At the surface g ≈ 10 Nkg⁻¹ with r = R, and at height h = R the distance from the centre is r' = R + h = 2R.
Therefore g' = g·(R/2R)² = g/4 = 10/4 = 2.5 Nkg⁻¹, so option A is correct.
Option D (10 Nkg⁻¹) assumes no change with altitude, but gravitational field strength decreases with increasing distance from the Earth's centre.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A body weighs 100 N on the Earth's surface. What does it weigh at the center of the Earth?
records.optionsJson: ["0 N","50 N","100 N","200 N © The Scholars Forge Tutorial | 350+ is ours! | Page 10 UTME '26 REVELATION | PHYSICS MASTERY PACK | 200 Questions | Tutor Dave ✓"]
records.explanation:
Weight is the gravitational force on a mass and equals m times the local gravitational field g.
For a spherically symmetric Earth the shell theorem shows only the mass enclosed within radius r contributes to gravity at that point and outer shells cancel out.
As r approaches zero the enclosed mass (∝ r^3) and hence g (∝ r) go to zero, so the gravitational field at the centre is exactly zero.
Option D (200 N) is baseless because vector contributions from all directions cancel at the centre, so the weight cannot increase there.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Newton's law of universal gravitation states that the gravitational force between two masses is
records.optionsJson: ["Directly proportional to the square of their distance apart","Inversely proportional to the product of their masses","Directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their distance","Independent of the distance between them ✓"]
records.explanation:
Newton's law of universal gravitation states the magnitude of the gravitational force between two point masses is F = Gm₁m₂/r².
This formula means the force is directly proportional to the product of the two masses, so increasing either mass increases the force proportionally.
The r² in the denominator makes the force inversely proportional to the square of the separation, so doubling the distance reduces the force to one quarter.
Option D is incorrect because the force clearly depends on distance through the 1/r² term and is not independent of separation.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: An astronaut in an orbiting spacecraft experiences weightlessness because
records.optionsJson: ["There is no gravitational force in space","The gravitational force and centripetal force balance","Both the spacecraft and astronaut are in free fall with the same acceleration","The spacecraft moves too fast for gravity to act ✓"]
records.explanation:
This question concerns weightlessness in orbit, which occurs when an object and its container undergo the same gravitational acceleration (free fall).
In orbit both the astronaut and spacecraft are continuously accelerated toward Earth by gravity while their forward speed keeps them on a curved path around the planet.
Because astronaut and craft accelerate together there is no contact (normal) force between them, so the astronaut experiences weightlessness despite gravity acting on both.
Option D is incorrect because high speed does not cancel gravity; the correct orbital speed simply makes the spacecraft continuously fall around Earth, producing free fall.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The gravitational potential at a point in a gravitational field is defined as
records.optionsJson: ["The force per unit mass at that point","The work done per unit mass in moving from infinity to that point","The total energy of a unit mass at that point","The acceleration due to gravity at that point"]
records.explanation:
Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to that point in the gravitational field.
This potential equals the potential energy per unit mass and for a point mass source is V = −GM/r, the negative sign showing the body is in a bound state relative to infinity.
Option B is correct because it matches the definition: work done per unit mass moving from infinity to the point.
Option D is incorrect because acceleration due to gravity refers to g (a vector magnitude GM/r^2), which is distinct from the scalar gravitational potential V.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Three concurrent forces are in equilibrium. If two of the forces are 8 N and 6 N at right angles to each other, the third force is
records.explanation:
Concurrent forces in equilibrium have a net vector sum of zero, so the third force must exactly balance the resultant of the other two.
With the two given forces at right angles, their resultant is found by Pythagoras: √(8^2 + 6^2) = √100 = 10 N.
Hence the third force must have magnitude 10 N and act opposite to that resultant to achieve equilibrium.
Option B (2 N) is the scalar difference relevant for collinear opposite forces, and option D (7 N) has no valid vector justification in this configuration.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The moment of a force about a point is defined as
records.optionsJson: ["Force divided by perpendicular distance","Force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force","The product of two equal and opposite forces","Force multiplied by any distance from the point ✓"]
records.explanation:
The moment (torque) of a force about a point is defined as the magnitude of the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
Perpendicular distance is the shortest distance to the line of action and the unit of moment is the newton‑metre (N·m).
Option B restates this definition exactly, so it is the correct choice.
Option D is incorrect because the distance must be the perpendicular distance; using any arbitrary distance generally yields a different (incorrect) moment unless that distance happens to be perpendicular.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A body is in stable equilibrium when
records.optionsJson: ["Its center of gravity is as high as possible","A slight displacement raises its center of gravity and it returns to original position","Any displacement keeps its center of gravity at the same height","A slight displacement lowers its center of gravity permanently ✓"]
records.explanation:
Stable equilibrium occurs when a small displacement produces a restoring force or moment that brings the body back to its original position.
Equivalently, a slight displacement raises the centre of gravity so gravitational potential energy increases and the body returns to the lower-energy equilibrium position.
Hence the correct option states the defining condition: a slight displacement raises the centre of gravity and the body returns to its original position.
Option D describes unstable equilibrium where a small displacement lowers the centre of gravity and the body moves further from the original position.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The equilibrant of two forces is
records.optionsJson: ["Equal in magnitude and same in direction as their resultant","The vector sum of the two forces","Equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to their resultant","The difference between the two forces ✓"]
records.explanation:
The equilibrant of two forces is the single force which, when added vectorially to those two forces, yields zero net force and so produces equilibrium.
By definition the resultant is the vector sum of the two forces, and the equilibrant must therefore have the same magnitude as that resultant but point in the opposite direction.
Option C is correct because a force equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the resultant cancels the resultant, giving R + E = 0.
Option D is wrong because the difference of the two forces does not in general equal the magnitude or direction required to cancel the resultant unless special conditions apply, so it cannot be assumed to be the equilibrant.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A machine has an efficiency of 80% and a velocity ratio of 5. Its mechanical advantage is
records.explanation:
The question uses the relationship between efficiency, mechanical advantage (MA) and velocity ratio (VR).
For simple machines efficiency (%) = (MA / VR) × 100, so MA = (efficiency × VR) / 100.
Substituting efficiency = 80% and VR = 5 gives MA = (80 × 5) / 100 = 4.
Option C (0.16) equals 0.8 ÷ 5 (efficiency as a fraction divided by VR) and option D (25) comes from an inappropriate multiplication (5 × 5); neither operation yields the MA.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A 60 W bulb is used for 10 hours daily. The electrical energy consumed in 30 days (in kWh) is
records.explanation:
Electrical energy used equals power multiplied by operating time, typically expressed in watt‑hours or kilowatt‑hours.
Here power = 60 W and total time = 10 h/day × 30 days = 300 h, so energy = 60 W × 300 h = 18,000 Wh = 18 kWh.
Option A, 18 kWh, matches this calculation and is therefore correct.
Option D, 0.18 kWh (180 Wh), arises if one wrongly divides instead of multiplying — it equals the energy of a 60 W lamp running for only 3 h rather than 300 h.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A car engine exerts a force of 2000 N and moves at 20 ms⁻¹. The power of the engine is
records.explanation:
Mechanical power for a force moving an object at constant speed is P = F × v, since power is the rate of doing work.
Substitute F = 2000 N and v = 20 m s⁻¹ to get P = 2000 × 20 = 40 000 W.
Convert watts to kilowatts: 40 000 W = 40 kW, so option A is correct.
Option D (4 W) is several orders of magnitude too small and has no basis in the correct calculation.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A body of mass 2 kg falls from rest through 5 m. Its kinetic energy just before hitting the ground is (g = 10 ms⁻²)
records.explanation:
Use conservation of mechanical energy: in free fall (neglecting air resistance) the loss in gravitational potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy.
Initial gravitational potential energy relative to the ground is mgh = 2 kg × 10 m/s² × 5 m = 100 J.
Therefore the kinetic energy just before impact is 100 J, so option A is correct.
Option D (10 J) corresponds to m×h = 2×5 and omits g, so it is incorrect.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The principle of conservation of energy states that
records.optionsJson: ["Energy can be created but not destroyed","Energy can be destroyed but not created","The total amount of energy in an isolated system remains constant","Kinetic energy always equals potential energy ✓"]
records.explanation:
The principle of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed but can be converted from one form to another.
Option C is correct because it restates this law: in an isolated system the total amount of energy (sum of all forms) remains constant.
Option A is wrong because claiming energy can be created contradicts the conservation law, and option B is wrong because claiming energy can be destroyed also contradicts it.
Example: in an ideal (frictionless) pendulum mechanical energy converts between KE and PE while the total (KE + PE) stays constant.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Solar energy is classified as a renewable energy source because
records.optionsJson: ["It can be stored indefinitely","It does not produce heat","It is continuously replenished by the sun and will not run out in human timescales","It is cheaper than coal ✓"]
records.explanation:
The question concerns classification of energy sources: 'renewable' means a resource is naturally replenished on human timescales rather than being exhausted by use.
Solar energy is classed as renewable because sunlight is supplied continuously by the Sun and is effectively inexhaustible within human timescales.
Option C is correct since the Sun will emit energy for billions of years, so using solar radiation does not deplete a finite stock of energy.
Option D is incorrect because economic cost does not determine whether a source is renewable; renewability is defined by natural replenishment rate, not price.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The area under a force-distance graph represents
records.optionsJson: ["Power","Work done","Acceleration","Momentum ✓"]
records.explanation:
Work is defined as the line integral of force along a displacement, W = ∫F·ds, so the area under an F–x graph represents the work done by that force over the displacement.
For a constant force the area is a rectangle (W = F·x) and for a variable force the area under the curve gives the equivalent integral; units are N·m or joules.
Power (option A) is the rate of doing work, P = dW/dt, and cannot be obtained from an F–x graph unless temporal information is supplied.
Therefore the correct choice is "work done" because an F–distance graph gives the integral of force over displacement while the alternatives involve time, mass, or velocity.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Static friction is always GREATER than kinetic (dynamic) friction because
records.optionsJson: ["Static surfaces have more area of contact","Intermolecular adhesive forces are stronger when surfaces are not sliding","Kinetic friction depends on velocity","Static surfaces are rougher"]
records.explanation:
The concept compares static friction (maximum fs,max = μsN) with kinetic friction (fk = μkN) and their typical magnitudes.
Static friction is usually greater because microscopic contact points and intermolecular adhesive bonds form when surfaces are at rest, requiring extra force to break when initiating motion.
During sliding many of these micro‑contacts are broken and reformed less effectively, so the average resisting force (μk) is smaller than the peak static value (μs).
Option D is also not the primary cause because roughness influences both coefficients, whereas the key reason static exceeds kinetic is the stronger adhesive/micro‑contact bonding at rest, making B correct.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A ball bearing falling through oil reaches terminal velocity when
records.optionsJson: ["Its weight equals the viscous drag plus upthrust","Its velocity becomes zero","The viscous drag force equals zero","Its acceleration is at maximum ✓"]
records.explanation:
Terminal velocity is reached when the net force on the falling sphere is zero so it falls at constant speed.
Therefore the weight (mg) is balanced by the sum of viscous drag and upthrust (buoyant force): weight = viscous drag + upthrust.
For small spheres in viscous liquids the drag increases with speed (Stokes' law: F = 6πηrv), so drag grows until it balances the effective weight.
Option C is wrong because viscous drag is zero only when speed is zero; at terminal speed the drag equals weight minus upthrust.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: According to Stokes' law, the viscous force on a sphere falling through a fluid is
records.optionsJson: ["F = 6πηrv","F = πηr²v","F = ηrv/6π","F = 6πη/rv ✓"]
records.explanation:
Stokes' law gives the viscous drag on a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid: F = 6πηrv.
Here η is the fluid's dynamic viscosity, r the sphere radius and v its speed; the law applies for laminar creeping flow with Reynolds number ≪ 1.
Option A is the standard result from solving the Stokes flow problem and therefore the correct expression, showing drag linear in r and v with numerical factor 6π.
Option D (6πη/rv) places r and v in the denominator and is dimensionally inconsistent with the expected increase of drag when r or v increases.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Which of the following is NOT a way to reduce friction?
records.optionsJson: ["Lubrication","Using ball bearings","Increasing the normal force between surfaces","Polishing the surfaces ✓"]
records.explanation:
Frictional force between two surfaces is given approximately by F = μN, so it depends on the coefficient of friction μ and the normal force N.
Increasing the normal force N increases F and therefore does not reduce friction, which is why option C is NOT a method to reduce friction.
Lubrication reduces friction by introducing a fluid film that separates microscopic contact points and lowers the effective coefficient μ.
Hence A, B and D are valid ways to reduce friction while increasing the normal force (C) increases friction, making C the correct answer.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A machine with velocity ratio 8 and efficiency 75% is used to lift a 200 N load. The effort required is
records.optionsJson: ["33.3 N","25 N","1200 N","18.75 N © The Scholars Forge Tutorial | 350+ is ours! | Page 16 UTME '26 REVELATION | PHYSICS MASTERY PACK | 200 Questions | Tutor Dave ✓"]
records.explanation:
The question involves mechanical advantage (MA), velocity ratio (VR) and efficiency where efficiency (%) = (MA/VR) × 100.
With VR = 8 and efficiency 75%, MA = VR × (efficiency/100) = 8 × 0.75 = 6.
Effort = Load / MA, so Effort = 200 N / 6 ≈ 33.3 N, which is option A.
Option D (18.75 N) results from an incorrect algebraic rearrangement of the efficiency relation and therefore yields an unrealistically low effort instead of the correct 33.3 N.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Which class of lever has the effort between the fulcrum and the load?
records.optionsJson: ["Class 1","Class 2","Class 3","All classes ✓"]
records.explanation:
A lever is a rigid bar that rotates about a fulcrum, with an effort applied at one point and a load at another.
In a class 3 lever the effort is placed between the fulcrum and the load, so option C is correct.
Third-class levers typically have mechanical advantage less than one and are used to increase speed or range of the load; a common example is the forearm where the biceps applies effort between the elbow (fulcrum) and the hand (load).
Hence options A and B are incorrect for the arrangement given, and D is incorrect because each lever class has a distinct fulcrum–effort–load order.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Why is the efficiency of a machine always less than 100%?
records.optionsJson: ["Machines always gain more energy than they use","Energy is lost in overcoming friction and moving parts of the machine itself","Velocity ratio is always greater than mechanical advantage","The load always moves faster than the effort ✓"]
records.explanation:
Efficiency is defined as (useful output work or energy ÷ input work or energy) × 100%, so the maximum possible efficiency is 100%.
Real machines always lose some input energy to friction between moving parts and to heating or accelerating parts of the machine itself, so useful output energy is always less than input energy.
Additional unavoidable losses such as air resistance, sound and internal deformations further reduce the output available for useful work.
Option D is incorrect because whether the load moves faster or slower than the effort depends on the machine design; in devices with MA>1 the load moves more slowly than the effort, not faster.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A spring of natural length 20 cm is extended by 5 cm when a force of 10 N is applied. The spring constant is
records.optionsJson: ["200 Nm⁻¹","2 Nm⁻¹","0.5 Nm⁻¹","50 Nm⁻¹ © The Scholars Forge Tutorial | 350+ is ours! | Page 17 UTME '26 REVELATION | PHYSICS MASTERY PACK | 200 Questions | Tutor Dave ✓"]
records.explanation:
Hooke's law gives F = k e for an elastic spring, with F in newtons, k in N·m⁻¹ and e in metres.
The extension is 5 cm, which must be converted to metres: e = 0.05 m.
Compute k = F/e = 10 N ÷ 0.05 m = 200 N·m⁻¹.
The natural length 20 cm is not used in calculating k here except to show the extension is 5 cm, and the result assumes the spring remains in the linear (Hookean) regime.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The elastic limit of a material is the point beyond which
records.optionsJson: ["The material obeys Hooke's law","The extension is proportional to force","The material does not return to its original shape when the load is removed","The material breaks immediately ✓"]
records.explanation:
The elastic limit is the maximum stress or load up to which a material returns to its original shape when the load is removed.
Beyond the elastic limit the material undergoes plastic (permanent) deformation and will not fully recover its original dimensions on unloading.
Hooke's law (force proportional to extension) holds only within the elastic limit, where deformation is elastic and reversible.
Option D is incorrect because breaking occurs at the ultimate or breaking point, which usually lies beyond the elastic limit and plastic region rather than at the elastic limit itself.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The work done in stretching a spring by extension e with spring constant k is
records.optionsJson: ["ke","2ke","½ke²","ke² ✓"]
records.explanation:
The question uses Hooke's law (F = kx) and the definition of mechanical work as area under the force–extension graph for a spring.
When a spring is stretched from 0 to e the force rises linearly from 0 to ke, so the graph is a right triangle with base e and height ke.
Work = area = ½ × base × height = ½ × e × ke = ½ke², which is the elastic potential energy stored in the spring.
Option D (ke²) has the correct units but lacks the ½ factor from the triangular area and therefore overestimates the work by a factor of two.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Young's modulus is defined as the ratio of
records.optionsJson: ["Stress to strain","Strain to stress","Force to area","Extension to original length ✓"]
records.explanation:
Young's modulus E is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain for a material when deformations remain within the elastic limit.
Mathematically E = (F/A)/(ΔL/L), where F is the applied force, A the cross‑sectional area, ΔL the extension and L the original length.
Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa) or N m⁻², and E quantifies the stiffness of a material in the elastic region.
Options C and D are wrong because C (force/area) is just stress, while D (extension/original length) is just strain; neither alone equals Young's modulus.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The pressure at a depth of 5 m in water is approximately (density of water = 1000 kgm⁻³, g = 10 ms⁻²)
records.explanation:
Hydrostatic pressure at depth is given by P = ρgh, where ρ is fluid density, g the gravitational acceleration and h the depth.
Substituting ρ = 1000 kg·m⁻³, g = 10 m·s⁻² and h = 5 m gives P = 1000×10×5 = 50,000 Pa.
Thus 50,000 Pa (50 kPa) is the gauge pressure due to the water column and matches option A.
The value given is gauge pressure from the water only; the absolute pressure would be this 50,000 Pa plus atmospheric pressure (≈101,000 Pa) if required.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Pascal's principle states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is
records.optionsJson: ["Transmitted equally to all parts of the fluid","Absorbed by the fluid","Proportional to the depth of the fluid","Inversely proportional to the volume ✓"]
records.explanation:
Pascal's principle states that a pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of its container.
Option A is correct because an external pressure on a confined fluid produces the same increase in pressure throughout the fluid, so all connected points experience an equal pressure change.
This uniform transmission of pressure is the operating principle behind hydraulic devices such as car brakes and hydraulic lifts, where a small force on a small-area piston gives a larger force on a larger-area piston.
Option D is wrong because pressure inversely proportional to volume describes Boyle's law for gases at constant temperature, not the transmission of pressure in a confined fluid.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A hydraulic press has a small piston of area 10 cm² and a large piston of area 200 cm². If a force of 50 N is applied to the small piston, the force exerted by the large piston is
records.explanation:
The question uses Pascal's principle: pressure is transmitted undiminished in a confined fluid so F1/A1 = F2/A2.
Rearrange to F2 = F1 × A2/A1 and substitute the values: F2 = 50 N × (200 cm² / 10 cm²).
This gives F2 = 50 × 20 = 1000 N, so option A (1000 N) is correct.
Option D (250 N) is incorrect as it introduces an extraneous factor of 4 or divides the correct result by 4; areas in cm² cancel so unit conversion is unnecessary.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A barometer can be used as an altimeter because
records.optionsJson: ["Mercury expands with altitude","Atmospheric pressure decreases with increasing altitude in a measurable way","Temperature decreases with altitude","Mercury pressure increases at higher altitudes ✓"]
records.explanation:
A mercury barometer measures atmospheric pressure by the height of a mercury column that is supported by the weight of the overlying air.
Atmospheric pressure decreases measurably with increasing altitude, so the mercury column falls as altitude increases and this change can be calibrated to give altitude.
Because the pressure–altitude relationship is predictable (expressed by the barometric formula), a calibrated barometer serves as an altimeter over the normal range of atmospheric conditions.
Option D is false and reversed: at higher altitudes atmospheric pressure (and therefore the supported mercury column) decreases rather than increases.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A solid displaces 200 cm³ of water when fully submerged. The upthrust on the solid is (density of water = 1000 kgm⁻³, g = 10 ms⁻²)
records.explanation:
The question concerns buoyancy: the upthrust on a submerged body equals the weight of the fluid displaced, F = ρVg.
Convert the volume to SI units: 200 cm³ = 200 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³.
Compute the upthrust: F = 1000 kg·m⁻³ × 2.0×10⁻⁴ m³ × 10 m·s⁻² = 2 N, so option A is correct.
Option D (200 N) is wrong as it implies a hundredfold volume or density error (e.g. using 0.02 m³ instead of 2.0×10⁻⁴ m³); correct unit conversion yields 2 N.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Archimedes' principle states that when a body is partially or fully immersed in a fluid, the upthrust equals
records.optionsJson: ["The weight of the body","The volume of fluid displaced","The weight of fluid displaced","The density of the fluid ✓"]
records.explanation:
Archimedes' principle states that a body partially or fully immersed in a fluid experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the body.
Therefore option C, 'the weight of fluid displaced', is correct because upthrust is a force measured in newtons and equals the displaced fluid's weight.
The upthrust is calculated from the displaced fluid mass m = ρV and gravity g, so U = m g = ρ V g, not simply a volume or density.
Option D is wrong because density alone cannot give an upthrust without the displaced volume (and gravity) to produce the weight of displaced fluid.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A ship floats because
records.optionsJson: ["Iron is less dense than water","The average density of the ship (including air spaces) is less than or equal to that of water","The ship is very heavy","Sea water has high salt content ✓"]
records.explanation:
Floating is governed by Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force on a body equals the weight of the fluid it displaces.
A ship's hull encloses large air spaces so its overall (average) density is less than or equal to that of water; it therefore displaces a volume of water whose weight balances the ship.
If the ship's average density is less than that of water it floats partly submerged; if equal it is neutrally buoyant when fully submerged.
Higher salinity increases seawater density and slightly aids buoyancy, but ships float mainly because their average density (including air spaces) is low, not because of salt content.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The temperature 37°C on the Kelvin scale is
records.explanation:
Use the Kelvin–Celsius relation K = °C + 273 (more precisely +273.15) to convert temperatures.
Applying this to 37°C gives 37 + 273 = 310 K, so option A is correct.
Option C (37 K) is wrong because it omits the +273 offset and treats the Celsius value as already in Kelvin.
Physically, 37°C is normal human body temperature and corresponds to about 310 K (more precisely 310.15 K).

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A thermometric property must
records.optionsJson: ["Vary linearly and measurably with temperature","Only change at fixed temperatures","Be a chemical property of matter","Remain constant over a temperature range"]
records.explanation:
A thermometric property is a physical quantity of a substance that changes in a measurable and reproducible way as temperature changes.
For practical thermometry the change should ideally be continuous and linear so equal increments of the property correspond to equal temperature intervals, simplifying calibration.
Option A is correct because a property that varies linearly and measurably with temperature allows a thermometer to be assigned uniform scale divisions and to read intermediate temperatures reliably.
Option D is wrong because a property that remains constant over a temperature range cannot indicate any temperature change and so cannot serve as a thermometric property.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Two fixed points used to calibrate a thermometer are
records.optionsJson: ["Boiling point of water and body temperature","Ice point (0°C) and steam point (100°C) at standard pressure","Absolute zero and body temperature","Room temperature and boiling point of oil ✓"]
records.explanation:
The concept is calibration of a Celsius thermometer using two fixed reproducible physical states of water.
The correct fixed points are the ice point (0°C), defined by melting pure ice in equilibrium with water, and the steam point (100°C), defined by boiling water at standard pressure (1 atm).
These two reproducible temperatures set the lower and upper reference marks of the Celsius scale for common laboratory thermometers.
Option D is incorrect since room temperature and boiling points of oils are not internationally standardized fixed points and can vary with composition and conditions.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A clinical thermometer has a constriction above the bulb. This is to
records.optionsJson: ["Prevent the mercury from returning to the bulb after removal from patient","Increase the sensitivity of the thermometer","Allow the thermometer to measure below 35°C","Prevent breakage of the thermometer ✓"]
records.explanation:
A clinical thermometer indicates temperature by the thermal expansion of mercury which rises in a narrow capillary above the bulb.
The constriction (kink) above the bulb traps the raised mercury column when the thermometer is removed from the patient so the reading is preserved.
When the bulb is warmed the mercury expands and flows past the kink, and surface tension at the constriction prevents the mercury from flowing back immediately into the bulb.
The kink is a trapping feature and does not prevent mechanical breakage; protection against breakage relies on casing and material, so option D is incorrect.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The relationship between linear expansivity (α), area expansivity (β) and volume expansivity (γ) is
records.optionsJson: ["β = α and γ = 2α","β = 2α and γ = 3α","β = 3α and γ = 2α","β = α/2 and γ = α/3 © The Scholars Forge Tutorial | 350+ is ours! | Page 22 UTME '26 REVELATION | PHYSICS MASTERY PACK | 200 Questions | Tutor Dave ✓"]
records.explanation:
Linear expansivity α is the fractional change in length per degree; area expansivity β and volume expansivity γ are fractional changes in area and volume per degree respectively.
For isotropic materials an original length L becomes L(1+αΔT), an area A becomes A(1+αΔT)^2 and a volume V becomes V(1+αΔT)^3 when temperature changes by ΔT.
For small temperature changes the binomial approximation (neglecting α^2 and higher terms) gives β ≈ 2α because (1+αΔT)^2 ≈ 1+2αΔT.
Options A and C merely swap the numerical coefficients and option D inverts them; all three contradict the binomial expansion result and are thus incorrect.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Expansion joints are provided in railway lines because
records.optionsJson: ["They make the tracks look better","Thermal expansion in hot weather would cause buckling without room to expand","They reduce the weight of the track","They absorb vibrations from trains ✓"]
records.explanation:
Rail tracks are made of steel which expands in length as temperature rises because of thermal expansion.
Without gaps or expansion joints the accumulated expansion stresses can force the rails to deform laterally and buckle, creating a derailment hazard.
Expansion joints provide controlled spaces at rail ends so each rail can move slightly and relieve compressive stress during hot weather.
Train vibrations are mainly absorbed by sleepers, ballast and fastenings, not by expansion joints, so option D is also incorrect.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Water has anomalous expansion because
records.optionsJson: ["It contracts on heating from 0°C to 4°C, reaching maximum density at 4°C","It expands on cooling from 4°C to 0°C, unlike most liquids","Both A and B are aspects of water's anomalous behavior","It becomes ice at 0°C and ice is less dense than water ✓"]
records.explanation:
Anomalous expansion of water means its density does not change monotonically with temperature around freezing, showing a maximum at 4°C.
Between 0°C and 4°C liquid water contracts on heating (its density increases) as some open hydrogen-bonded structures collapse, giving maximum density at 4°C.
On cooling from 4°C down to 0°C water expands (density decreases) because hydrogen bonding increasingly favors a more open, tetrahedral arrangement of molecules.
The underlying cause is hydrogen bonding that stabilizes expanded, ice-like networks at low temperature, producing expansion below 4°C and maximum density at 4°C.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The real expansivity of a liquid is related to apparent expansivity by
records.optionsJson: ["Real = Apparent + Expansivity of container material","Real = Apparent − Expansivity of container","Real = Apparent × Expansivity of container","Real = Apparent / Expansivity of container ✓"]
records.explanation:
Apparent expansivity is the observed fractional increase in the liquid's volume relative to the container, while the real expansivity is the liquid's actual fractional volume change. Because the container itself expands on heating, the observed (apparent) expansion equals the real expansion minus the container's cubic expansion. Rearranging that relationship yields Real = Apparent + expansivity of the container, which is option A. Option B would incorrectly subtract the container effect again and thus understate the liquid's true expansion. Options C and D are wrong because small fractional volume changes combine by addition/subtraction, not by multiplication or division. The container expansivity referred to is the cubical expansivity of the material (if only linear coefficient α is given, the cubical expansivity ≈ 3α).
confidence
high

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A gas at 27°C has a volume of 5 L at a pressure of 2 atm. What is its volume at 127°C and 4 atm?
records.optionsJson: ["3.33 L","2.5 L","10 L","6.67 L © The Scholars Forge Tutorial | 350+ is ours! | Page 23 UTME '26 REVELATION | PHYSICS MASTERY PACK | 200 Questions | Tutor Dave ✓"]
records.explanation:
Use the combined gas law for a fixed amount of ideal gas: P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2.
Convert temperatures to kelvin: T1 = 27°C = 300 K and T2 = 127°C = 400 K, then solve for V2.
V2 = P1V1T2/(P2T1) = (2×5×400)/(4×300) = 4000/1200 = 3.33 L, so option A is correct.
Option C (10 L) is inconsistent with the given pressure and temperature changes and would result only from an incorrect combination of errors or arithmetic, so it is not correct.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Boyle's law states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature
records.optionsJson: ["Pressure is directly proportional to volume","Pressure is inversely proportional to volume","Volume is directly proportional to temperature","Pressure is directly proportional to temperature ✓"]
records.explanation:
Boyle's law for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature states PV = constant.
Rearranging gives P ∝ 1/V, so pressure varies inversely with volume (e.g. halving V doubles P).
Because temperature is held constant the process is isothermal and internal energy change for an ideal gas is zero in the simple model.
Option C describes Charles' law (V ∝ T at constant pressure) and option D describes the pressure–temperature law (P ∝ T at constant volume), so neither applies here.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The temperature at which a gas would theoretically have zero volume or zero pressure is called
records.optionsJson: ["Critical temperature","Absolute zero","Melting point","Dew point ✓"]
records.explanation:
The correct term is absolute zero, defined as 0 K (−273.15°C), the theoretical temperature where a system has minimum thermal kinetic energy.
By the ideal gas law PV = nRT, if temperature T is extrapolated to zero then, depending on the constraint (fixed P or fixed V), either volume V or pressure P would tend toward zero, which justifies the choice.
Absolute zero is a theoretical lower limit in thermodynamics and cannot be reached in practice, but it is the temperature referenced when speaking of zero gas pressure or volume in idealised models.
Dew point is the temperature at which air reaches saturation and vapour condenses; it does not describe the gas law limit of zero pressure or volume.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Charles' law states that at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is
records.optionsJson: ["Inversely proportional to its Kelvin temperature","Directly proportional to its Kelvin temperature","Directly proportional to its Celsius temperature","Independent of temperature"]
records.explanation:
Charles's law states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure, V/T = constant, so the volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
From the ideal gas law PV = nRT, rearranging gives V = (nR/P)T, which mathematically shows V ∝ T when P and n are constant.
The correct option is 'directly proportional to its Kelvin temperature' because Kelvin is the absolute temperature scale starting at zero kinetic energy, required for proportionality.
Option D is wrong because at constant pressure a gas's volume does change with temperature — heating expands the gas and cooling contracts it.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A van der Waals gas differs from an ideal gas because
records.optionsJson: ["Its molecules have finite size and experience intermolecular forces","Its molecules have zero size","It obeys PV = nRT exactly","Temperature has no effect on it ✓"]
records.explanation:
The van der Waals model modifies the ideal gas law by introducing correction terms to describe real-gas behaviour.
Its general equation (P + a n^2/V^2)(V − n b) = nRT introduces the constant a for intermolecular attractions and b for finite molecular volume.
Option A is correct because b represents the excluded volume of molecules and a reduces the effective pressure by accounting for attractive forces between particles.
Option D is false because temperature changes molecular kinetic energy and therefore affects the pressure and behaviour of both ideal and real gases.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: 5 kg of water is heated from 20°C to 80°C. The heat energy absorbed is (specific heat capacity of water = 4200 Jkg⁻¹K⁻¹)
records.explanation:
Heat required to raise the temperature of a substance is Q = m c ΔT, where m is mass, c is specific heat capacity and ΔT is the temperature change.
For this problem m = 5 kg, c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and ΔT = 80 − 20 = 60 K, so Q = 5 × 4200 × 60.
Carrying out the multiplication gives Q = 1,260,000 J = 1.26 MJ, which is option A.
Option D (252,000 J) does not follow from the given values; it would arise from using an incorrect ΔT (≈12 K) or a different mass and is therefore wrong.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 336,000 Jkg⁻¹. The heat required to melt 500 g of ice at 0°C is
records.explanation:
This question uses the specific latent heat of fusion Lf, the energy required to melt 1 kg of a substance at its melting point without temperature change (units J kg⁻¹).
Apply Q = mLf and convert the mass 500 g to 0.5 kg before computing.
Substituting gives Q = 0.5 kg × 336,000 J kg⁻¹ = 168,000 J, therefore option A is correct.
Option D (336,000 J) equals Lf for 1 kg and thus incorrectly treats the sample as 1 kg instead of 0.5 kg.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Boiling differs from evaporation in that boiling
records.optionsJson: ["Occurs only at the surface of a liquid","Occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature and produces bubbles","Occurs at any temperature","Requires less energy than evaporation"]
records.explanation:
Boiling is rapid vaporization that occurs when a liquid's vapor pressure equals the external pressure, producing vapor bubbles throughout the bulk of the liquid.
At a given external pressure the boiling point is a specific temperature, so boiling proceeds at that fixed temperature until phase change conditions change.
Evaporation is a surface phenomenon that can occur at temperatures below the boiling point and does not produce bubbles within the liquid.
Option D is incorrect because boiling requires the latent heat of vaporization per unit mass comparable to evaporation and is not inherently a lower-energy process.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Increasing pressure on the surface of a boiling liquid will
records.optionsJson: ["Lower the boiling point","Raise the boiling point","Have no effect on boiling point","Cause immediate solidification ✓"]
records.explanation:
Boiling occurs when the vapor pressure of a liquid equals the external (atmospheric) pressure at its surface.
Increasing the external pressure raises the vapor pressure required for bubbles to form, so a higher temperature (boiling point) is needed.
Therefore option B is correct: raising external pressure raises the boiling point, as used in pressure cookers to increase cooking temperature.
Option D is wrong because increased pressure raises the boiling temperature and does not cause immediate solidification; solidification depends on temperature and the material's phase diagram.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A pressure cooker raises the boiling point of water above 100°C. This means that food cooks faster because
records.optionsJson: ["The water contains more pressure energy","The higher temperature increases the rate of chemical reactions in cooking","The steam is drier","Less water is needed ✓"]
records.explanation:
A pressure cooker raises the internal pressure so water and steam inside can reach temperatures above 100°C (typical working values are around 120°C).
Because chemical reaction rates increase with temperature, the higher temperature inside a pressure cooker makes the cooking reactions in food proceed faster.
This is consistent with the senior‑secondary Arrhenius idea that many reaction rates increase markedly with temperature (a rough rule of thumb is that rates double for every 10°C rise).
Option D is incorrect because simply using less water does not explain the increased reaction rates; the key factor is the higher boiling temperature produced by the raised pressure.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Relative humidity is defined as the ratio of
records.optionsJson: ["Actual mass of water vapor in air to mass of water vapor needed to saturate the same air at the same temperature","Temperature of air to dew point temperature © The Scholars Forge Tutorial | 350+ is ours! | Page 26 UTME '26 REVELATION | PHYSICS MASTERY PACK | 200 Questions | Tutor Dave","Pressure of water vapor to atmospheric pressure","Volume of water vapor to volume of dry air ✓"]
records.explanation:
Relative humidity is the ratio of the actual mass (or partial pressure) of water vapour in air to the mass (or saturation vapour pressure) required to saturate the same air at the same temperature, usually expressed as a percentage.
Option A restates this definition correctly by comparing the actual water-vapour mass to the mass needed for saturation at that temperature.
An equivalent expression used in senior-secondary physics is RH = e/e_s × 100%, where e is the actual vapour pressure and e_s is the saturation vapour pressure at the same temperature.
Option D is not the standard definition: while vapour volume can relate to mass under fixed conditions, relative humidity is defined by mass or vapour pressure relative to saturation, not a simple volume ratio.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The dew point is the temperature at which
records.optionsJson: ["All water vapor condenses into rain","The water vapor in air becomes saturated (SVP equals actual vapor pressure)","Ice forms on surfaces","Humidity is 0% ✓"]
records.explanation:
The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated with its current amount of water vapour so that saturation vapour pressure equals the actual vapour pressure.
At the dew point the relative humidity is 100% and further cooling causes condensation onto surfaces or cloud formation.
Option B is correct because it gives the definition in terms of vapour pressures (SVP = actual vapour pressure), which is the standard thermodynamic description of dew point.
Option D is incorrect because humidity at the dew point is 100%, whereas 0% indicates completely dry air, the opposite condition.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A wet and dry bulb hygrometer shows wet bulb temperature of 18°C and dry bulb temperature of 24°C. The difference indicates
records.optionsJson: ["The temperature has risen","Evaporation is occurring from the wet bulb, indicating unsaturated air with RH < 100%","The air is fully saturated","It is raining outside ✓"]
records.explanation:
A wet-and-dry bulb hygrometer compares a dry-bulb temperature and a wet-bulb temperature to assess atmospheric humidity.
Evaporation from the wet bulb absorbs latent heat and cools it, so a wet-bulb reading of 18°C versus a dry-bulb 24°C shows evaporation is occurring.
The 6°C depression indicates the air is unsaturated and the relative humidity is less than 100%; greater wet–dry differences correspond to drier air.
You also cannot conclude it is raining from this reading; precipitation requires additional meteorological evidence and is not indicated solely by wet-bulb depression.

records.subject: Physics
records.topic: Structure of matter and kinetic theory
records.question: Brownian motion provides evidence for
records.optionsJson: ["The wave nature of matter","The continuous and random motion of molecules in a fluid","The existence of atoms only in solids","The absence of intermolecular forces ✓"]
records.explanation:
Brownian motion is the erratic, random movement of microscopic particles suspended in a fluid, observable under a microscope.
This movement results from continual, unequal impacts by the fluid's molecules, which themselves are in random thermal motion.
Hence option B is correct: Brownian motion provides direct evidence that molecules in a fluid undergo continuous and random motion.
Option D is false because Brownian motion arises from molecular collisions and thermal motion, which presuppose interacting molecules rather than an absence of intermolecular forces.

records.subject: Physics
records.topic: Structure of matter and kinetic theory
records.question: Surface tension is explained by molecular theory as arising from
records.optionsJson: ["Gravity acting on surface molecules","Cohesion between molecules at the surface and net inward molecular force due to unbalanced cohesive forces","Adhesion of water to air molecules","The low density of surface molecules ✓"]
records.explanation:
Surface tension arises because molecules inside a liquid are pulled equally in all directions by cohesive forces, while molecules at the surface lack neighbors above and therefore experience a net inward cohesive force.
This unbalanced cohesive force tends to minimize the liquid's surface area and appears macroscopically as a contractile 'skin', measurable as force per unit length or as surface energy per unit area.
Option B correctly states the molecular origin: cohesion among surface molecules and the resulting inward force produce surface tension.
The idea of lower surface density (option D) is misleading: surface tension is due to unbalanced intermolecular forces at the interface, not to a lower density of surface molecules.

records.subject: Physics
records.topic: Structure of matter and kinetic theory
records.question: Diffusion occurs more rapidly in gases than in liquids because
records.optionsJson: ["Gas molecules are heavier","Gas molecules have larger intermolecular distances and higher average speeds","Liquids are more viscous than solids","Gas molecules have stronger intermolecular forces ✓"]
records.explanation:
Diffusion is the net movement of particles from regions of higher concentration to lower concentration driven by random thermal motion of molecules (kinetic theory).
In gases molecules are widely spaced so the mean free path is large and, at typical temperatures, they have high average speeds (order of 10^2 m/s), allowing rapid mixing.
In liquids molecules are closely packed with frequent collisions and stronger intermolecular attractions, which reduce molecular mobility and slow diffusion.
Option C is irrelevant to the gas–liquid comparison (viscosity of liquids vs solids does not explain why gases diffuse faster) and option D is false because gases have weaker, not stronger, intermolecular forces than liquids.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Capillarity (capillary action) occurs because of
records.optionsJson: ["Only cohesion between liquid molecules","The interplay between adhesion (liquid to tube) and cohesion (liquid to liquid) forces","Atmospheric pressure pushing liquid up the tube","The weight of liquid in the tube ✓"]
records.explanation:
Capillarity is the spontaneous rise or fall of a liquid in a narrow tube caused by surface tension arising from molecular adhesion and cohesion.
The correct option is the interplay between adhesion (liquid-to-tube) and cohesion (liquid-to-liquid): when adhesion exceeds cohesion the liquid climbs the tube and forms a concave meniscus, and when cohesion exceeds adhesion the liquid is depressed with a convex meniscus.
For example, water wets glass (adhesion > cohesion) so it rises in a capillary, whereas mercury does not wet glass (cohesion > adhesion) so it is depressed.
The weight of the liquid opposes capillary rise; an equilibrium height is reached when the upward force from surface tension (due to adhesion/cohesion) balances the downward weight of the liquid column.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: In a vacuum flask (thermos flask), heat loss by radiation is minimized by
records.optionsJson: ["The double glass walls","The silvered inner surfaces which reflect radiated heat","The stopper at the top","The outer casing ✓"]
records.explanation:
A vacuum flask reduces heat transfer by addressing the three modes of heat flow: conduction, convection and radiation.
The silvered inner surfaces are correct because they reflect infrared radiation back into the flask, greatly reducing radiative heat loss.
The vacuum between the double walls prevents conduction and convection because there are no particles to carry heat across the gap.
Option D (the outer casing) mainly provides mechanical protection and minimal insulation; it is not the primary means of reducing radiative heat loss.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Heat transfer by convection requires
records.optionsJson: ["A vacuum","A medium and bulk movement of the fluid carrying thermal energy","Contact between two solid surfaces","Electromagnetic radiation ✓"]
records.explanation:
Convection is heat transfer that occurs by bulk motion of a fluid (liquid or gas) carrying thermal energy from one place to another.
It depends on density differences caused by temperature: warmer fluid becomes less dense and rises while cooler, denser fluid sinks, forming convection currents.
Because convection requires the motion of fluid particles it cannot occur in a vacuum and therefore needs a material medium.
Therefore the correct option is 'a medium and bulk movement of the fluid carrying thermal energy'; the other choices describe conduction, vacuum conditions, or radiation and so are incorrect.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A good absorber of heat radiation is also a good
records.optionsJson: ["Reflector","Emitter","Conductor","Insulator ✓"]
records.explanation:
Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation states that, for a body in thermal equilibrium, absorptivity equals emissivity at each wavelength and direction.
Therefore a good absorber of heat radiation must also be a good emitter of radiation at the same temperature.
A perfect absorber (black body) absorbs all incident radiation and is also the ideal emitter for thermal radiation.
Thus the correct choice is 'Emitter'; the other options are incorrect because reflectors are poor absorbers and conduction/insulation are different heat-transfer processes.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Land breeze occurs at night because
records.optionsJson: ["The sea heats up faster than land and the warm air rises over the sea","The land cools down faster than sea at night, so warm air rises over sea and cool air from land moves to replace it","The land is always warmer than the sea","Wind always blows from sea to land © The Scholars Forge Tutorial | 350+ is ours! | Page 29 UTME '26 REVELATION | PHYSICS MASTERY PACK | 200 Questions | Tutor Dave ✓"]
records.explanation:
At night the land loses heat faster than the sea, so the sea surface remains relatively warmer.
Warmer air above the sea becomes less dense and rises, producing a local low pressure over the water.
Cooler, denser air over the land flows toward the sea to replace the rising warm air, creating a wind from land to sea called a land breeze.
Options C and D are false generalisations: land is not always warmer than sea, and winds do not always blow from sea to land regardless of diurnal heating.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The rate of heat conduction through a material is increased by
records.optionsJson: ["Decreasing the temperature gradient","Increasing the thickness of the material","Increasing the cross-sectional area and temperature gradient","Using a material with low thermal conductivity ✓"]
records.explanation:
Heat conduction in solids is given by Fourier's law Q/t = kA(ΔT/L), relating heat flow rate to thermal conductivity k, area A, temperature difference ΔT and thickness L.
In this relation k is the material's thermal conductivity, A is the cross-sectional area, ΔT is the temperature difference, and the temperature gradient is ΔT/L.
Option C is correct because Q/t is directly proportional to both A and the temperature gradient, so increasing either increases the rate of heat transfer.
Option D is incorrect because a material with low thermal conductivity k produces a smaller Q/t compared with a material of higher k under the same A, ΔT and L.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The frequency of a wave is 500 Hz and its wavelength is 0.4 m. The velocity of the wave is
records.explanation:
The relevant relation is v = fλ, where v is wave speed, f is frequency and λ is wavelength.
Substituting f = 500 Hz and λ = 0.4 m gives v = 500 × 0.4 = 200 m s⁻¹.
Unit check: Hz is s⁻¹ so (s⁻¹)(m) = m s⁻¹, confirming the correct unit for speed.
Option D (2000 m s⁻¹) is an arithmetic slip (e.g. multiplying 500 by 4 instead of 0.4) and is also incorrect.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Polarization of waves is only possible for
records.optionsJson: ["Longitudinal waves","Sound waves","Transverse waves","All types of waves ✓"]
records.explanation:
Polarization means restricting the oscillation directions of a wave to a particular plane or orientation.
This restriction is possible only when oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation, i.e. for transverse waves.
Transverse waves such as electromagnetic waves (light) therefore can be polarized, so option C is correct.
Option D is wrong because not all waves are transverse; only transverse waves exhibit polarization and practical polarizers (e.g. polarizing filters) demonstrate this property.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Beat frequency is produced when two sound waves of frequencies 440 Hz and 444 Hz are sounded together. The beat frequency is
records.explanation:
Beat frequency arises when two sound waves of nearly equal frequency interfere and equals the absolute difference of their frequencies.
For 440 Hz and 444 Hz the beat frequency is |440 − 444| = 4 Hz, so four loudness pulses are heard each second.
These beats are amplitude modulation of the combined signal, not a new steady tone at the sum frequency.
Option D (2 Hz) is wrong because there is no reason to halve the difference; beats equal the full absolute difference, 4 Hz.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Sound travels faster in
records.optionsJson: ["Vacuum","Air","Water","Steel ✓"]
records.explanation:
The speed of sound in a medium depends on that medium's elasticity (stiffness) and density, with higher stiffness generally increasing wave speed.
Solids such as steel have a very high elastic (Young's) modulus, so longitudinal sound waves in steel travel much faster (on the order of 5000 m s⁻¹) than in liquids or gases.
Water is less compressible and denser than air, so sound travels faster in water (around 1500 m s⁻¹ in seawater) than in air.
Thus, among the options given the correct choice is steel, consistent with the general ordering solids > liquids > gases for sound speed.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: An echo is heard 2 seconds after a sound is produced. If the speed of sound in air is 340 ms⁻¹, the distance to the reflecting surface is
records.explanation:
An echo heard 2 s after a sound is the reflected wave whose total travel time to the reflector and back is 2 s.
The total distance travelled by the sound equals speed × time = 340 m/s × 2 s = 680 m.
The reflecting surface is halfway along that round trip, so the one-way distance = 680 m ÷ 2 = 340 m.
Options C (170 m) and D (85 m) are incorrect: 170 m would follow from using 1 s or halving again incorrectly, and 85 m has no basis in the round-trip calculation.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The pitch of a musical note is determined by its
records.optionsJson: ["Amplitude","Intensity","Frequency","Waveform ✓"]
records.explanation:
Pitch is the perceived highness or lowness of a sound and is primarily related to the sound wave's frequency.
Frequency, measured in hertz (Hz), indicates how many vibrations occur per second; higher frequency produces a higher pitch.
Amplitude affects loudness; a larger amplitude makes a sound seem louder but does not change its pitch.
Thus Frequency is correct because it directly controls pitch, while amplitude and intensity govern loudness and waveform governs timbre.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A closed pipe of length 0.5 m resonates in its fundamental mode. The frequency of the note produced is (speed of sound = 340 ms⁻¹)
records.optionsJson: ["170 Hz","340 Hz © The Scholars Forge Tutorial | 350+ is ours! | Page 32 UTME '26 REVELATION | PHYSICS MASTERY PACK | 200 Questions | Tutor Dave","680 Hz","85 Hz ✓"]
records.explanation:
This question concerns standing waves in a pipe closed at one end, where the fundamental mode has the pipe length equal to one quarter of a wavelength (L = λ/4).
For a closed pipe the fundamental frequency is therefore f = v/(4L) because only odd quarter‑wavelength harmonics (1, 3, 5, ...) are allowed.
Substituting v = 340 m/s and L = 0.5 m gives f = 340/(4×0.5) = 340/2 = 170 Hz, so option A is correct.
Because closed pipes support only odd harmonics, the next resonant frequency after 170 Hz would be the 3rd harmonic at 3×170 = 510 Hz.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Reverberation differs from echo in that
records.optionsJson: ["Reverberation is heard as a distinct separate sound","Reverberation is the persistence of sound due to multiple reflections in an enclosed space","Echo is caused by multiple reflections","Reverberation occurs outdoors only ✓"]
records.explanation:
Reverberation is the persistence of sound produced when many reflections from walls and objects in an enclosed space arrive so close together that they merge and prolong the original sound.
The correct option (B) is right because reverberation involves multiple rapid reflections in halls or rooms that blend into a continuous decay rather than distinct repeats.
An echo is a distinct separate reflection heard when the reflected sound is delayed sufficiently from the direct sound, typically more than about 0.1 s (requiring the reflector to be roughly 17 m or more away).
Option D is wrong because reverberation is characteristic of enclosed or partially enclosed spaces (indoors), not exclusively outdoors.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The fundamental frequency of a vibrating string is increased by
records.optionsJson: ["Increasing the length of the string","Decreasing the tension in the string","Increasing the tension or decreasing the length or using a lighter string","Increasing the mass per unit length ✓"]
records.explanation:
A vibrating string's fundamental frequency is given by f = (1/2L)√(T/μ), where L is length, T the tension and μ the mass per unit length.
From this relation frequency increases with the square root of tension, decreases inversely with length, and increases when mass per unit length decreases.
Therefore option C is correct because raising tension, shortening the string or using a lighter string (smaller μ) all raise the fundamental frequency.
Option D is wrong because increasing the mass per unit length lowers the frequency (f ∝ 1/√μ), so a heavier string gives a lower fundamental frequency.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The image formed by a pinhole camera is
records.optionsJson: ["Virtual, upright, and magnified","Real, inverted, and diminished or magnified depending on distances","Virtual, inverted, and always diminished","Real, upright, and always magnified ✓"]
records.explanation:
A pinhole camera produces a real image because light rays from an object pass through the tiny aperture and converge on a screen where they meet.
Rays from the top and bottom of the object cross at the pinhole, so the image formed on the screen is inverted.
By similar triangles the linear magnification m = image distance/object distance, so the image size can be diminished or magnified depending on those distances.
Options C and D are incorrect because C mislabels the image as virtual and always diminished, while D wrongly claims the image is upright and always magnified, both contradicting ray-crossing geometry and the distance-dependent magnification.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A concave mirror has a focal length of 15 cm. An object is placed 10 cm in front of it. The image is
records.optionsJson: ["Real, inverted, at 30 cm behind the mirror","Virtual, upright, 30 cm behind the mirror","At infinity © The Scholars Forge Tutorial | 350+ is ours! | Page 33 UTME '26 REVELATION | PHYSICS MASTERY PACK | 200 Questions | Tutor Dave","Real at 6 cm in front ✓"]
records.explanation:
A concave mirror with focal length 15 cm and an object placed 10 cm (inside the focal length) produces a virtual, upright and magnified image, as predicted by the spherical mirror equation.
Solving 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with f = 15 cm and u = 10 cm yields |v| = 30 cm, so the image is 30 cm behind the mirror (virtual) when a consistent sign convention is used.
The magnification is 3 (|v/u| = 30/10 = 3), and since the image is virtual its orientation is upright rather than inverted.
Option D is incorrect both numerically and conceptually: the mirror equation does not give a 6 cm image in front of the mirror and a real image in front would require the object to be outside the focal length.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The laws of reflection state that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and both angles are measured
records.optionsJson: ["From the reflecting surface","From the normal to the surface at the point of incidence","From the horizontal","From each other ✓"]
records.explanation:
The laws of reflection state that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and both angles are measured with respect to the normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence.
The normal is an imaginary line drawn perpendicular to the surface at the point where the light ray strikes, and it provides the standard reference for measuring those angles.
Measuring angles from the normal ensures the equality holds regardless of how the surface is tilted, so the relation is independent of the mirror's orientation.
Option D is incorrect since the incident and reflected angles are each measured from the same normal line, not from each other, and therefore are equal in magnitude.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A convex mirror always forms images that are
records.optionsJson: ["Real, inverted, and diminished","Virtual, upright, and diminished regardless of object position","Real, upright, and magnified","Virtual, inverted, and magnified ✓"]
records.explanation:
A convex (diverging) mirror causes parallel rays to diverge as if they came from a focal point located behind the mirror.
Because the reflected rays diverge, their backward extensions meet behind the mirror and form an image that cannot be projected on a screen (a virtual image).
Using the mirror equation and magnification, the image distance lies behind the mirror and the lateral magnification |m| is less than 1, so the image is upright and diminished for any real object position.
Option D is wrong because convex mirrors do not produce inverted or magnified images for real objects (a magnified virtual upright image can occur with a concave mirror when the object is between the focus and the mirror).

records.subject: Physics
records.question: When light passes from air into glass, it bends toward the normal because
records.optionsJson: ["Light speeds up in glass","Light slows down in glass (denser medium) and the wavefront is refracted","The wavelength increases in glass","The frequency changes in glass ✓"]
records.explanation:
Refraction is the change in direction of a wave when it passes obliquely between media in which its propagation speed differs.
When light goes from air into glass it slows down because glass has higher optical density and refractive index n = c/v > 1.
By Huygens' principle the part of the wavefront that enters the glass first slows while the rest keeps moving, so the wavefront pivots and the ray bends toward the normal.
Option D is incorrect because frequency is set by the source and remains constant across the boundary; only the wave’s speed and wavelength change.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: The critical angle for glass-air interface is related to refractive index n by
records.optionsJson: ["sin C = n","sin C = 1/n","cos C = n","tan C = n ✓"]
records.explanation:
The critical angle C at a glass–air boundary is the angle of incidence in glass for which the refracted ray grazes the interface (refracted angle 90°), beyond which total internal reflection occurs.
Using Snell's law n_glass·sin C = n_air·sin 90° gives n·sin C = 1, hence sin C = 1/n, so option B is correct.
Option A (sin C = n) is impossible for typical glass since n>1 would require sin C>1, which cannot occur.
Remember that a meaningful critical angle exists only when light goes from a denser medium (n>1) to a rarer one (n≈1), so sin C = 1/n yields a real C for such cases.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: A converging lens has a focal length of 20 cm. An object is placed 30 cm from the lens. The image distance is
records.optionsJson: ["60 cm on the same side as the object","60 cm on the opposite side from the object","12 cm","120 cm ✓"]
records.explanation:
Use the thin lens formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with f taken as +20 cm for a converging lens and u = +30 cm for an object 30 cm from the lens.
Substitute the values: 1/20 = 1/30 + 1/v.
Rearranging gives 1/v = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60, so v = 60 cm.
Option C (12 cm) comes from the algebraic error 1/v = 1/f + 1/u, and option D (120 cm) is an arithmetic or sign mistake.

records.subject: Physics
records.question: Dispersion of white light by a prism occurs because
